en: The *Mahāyānaviṃśikā-śāstra*,
composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna;
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
I take refuge in the inconceivable nature, the unattached, true wisdom of all Buddhas;
though all phenomena are neither expressible nor inexpressible, the Buddha has skillfully proclaimed them out of his great compassion.
The ultimate truth is non-arising; though it follows along with the turning of phenomena, it lacks intrinsic nature.
Buddhas and sentient beings share a single characteristic, equal like space.
This shore and the other shore are non-arising, for their self-nature is born of conditions.
All those conditioned phenomena are empty; they are the practice of the wisdom of all-knowledge.
Their nature is stainless *tathatā*, non-dual, and quiescent.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like a reflection, without distinction.
The discriminative mind of ordinary beings falsely conceives of a self where no real self exists;
thus they give rise to various afflictions, as well as suffering, pleasure, equanimity, and so forth.
The aging, illness, and death of the world are suffering and undesirable.
Falling and plummeting according to one's various karmas, there is truly no happiness here.
The supreme and wondrous bliss of the celestial realms and the extreme suffering of the hells are all unreal domains;
one constantly revolves through the six destinies.
Sentient beings engage in false conceptualization, Burned by the fires of affliction,
they fall into realms such as the hells, Like wild fires consuming a forest.
Sentient beings are fundamentally illusory, Yet they further grasp at illusory objects.
Treading the path created by illusion, one does not understand that it arises from conditions.
Like a worldly painter who draws the form of a yakṣa and is terrified by what he himself has painted— this is called a person of no wisdom.
Sentient beings give rise to defilement themselves, creating the causes for that saṃsāra;
having created them, they fear falling into it, yet lacking wisdom, they do not attain liberation.
With deluded and false minds, sentient beings give rise to the stains of doubt and confusion.
Those who perceive existence where there is no inherent nature endure the most extreme suffering among all sufferings.
Seeing that they have no refuge, the Buddha gave rise to a mind of compassion;
thus he resolved upon bodhicitta and extensively cultivated the practices of enlightenment.
Having attained the fruit of unsurpassed wisdom, he observes the world and sees how beings are entangled by conceptual discrimination; therefore, he acts for their benefit.
From birth until after birth, he reveals the meaning of perfect truth to all.
Later, one contemplates that the world is empty, devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
One contemplates birth-and-death and nirvāṇa; both of these are without self.
They are neither defiled nor subject to destruction; they are fundamentally pure and eternally quiescent.
All the realms within a dream, once one has awakened, are seen no more;
so too the wise, having woken from the sleep of delusion, see neither birth nor death.
Those shrouded by the darkness of ignorance fall into the ocean of birth and death.
Without birth, they conceive of birth, giving rise to worldly discrimination.
If they discriminate that there is birth, sentient beings act unreasonably;
within the phenomena of birth and death, they give rise to the notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
All this is but mind alone, established as illusory manifestations;
by performing wholesome or unwholesome karma, one experiences wholesome or unwholesome births.
If the wheel of the mind is extinguished, then all phenomena are extinguished.
These dharmas are without self; all dharmas are entirely pure.
The Buddha has extensively proclaimed the worldly dharmas—know that these are conditioned by ignorance.
If one can give rise to no mind of discrimination, from what could any sentient being be born?
Within the dharmatā of all those phenomena, one cannot find even the slightest dharma upon thorough investigation;
just as a worldly magician performs illusory feats, so should the wise understand.
Within the great ocean of the cycle of birth and death, the waters of sentient beings' afflictions are full;
if one does not transport them by means of the Mahāyāna, how could they ever reach the further shore?
The Treatise in Twenty Verses on the Mahāyāna (Mahāyānaviṃśikā-śāstra)
